title: How do you plan a product launch in a case interview?
description: "How should the client launch the product?" The client wants a plan to launch a product. If the question is whether to launch at all, use market entry.
hook: Plan a product launch in four steps: choose who to target, design what to offer (product, price, place and promotion), decide how to roll it out, and check that it pays. The order matters, because every choice about the offer follows from the customer you picked first.
body:
When you will use it

The client has decided to launch something and wants a plan: "How should we launch our new protein bar?" If the question is whether to launch at all, start with the market entry structure and come back to this once the answer is yes.

This is a generate question: "How can we do this?" Lay out the choices in buckets that do not overlap, size them, then pick the best. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Who is it for, and what does the launch need to achieve: trial, repeat customers, market share or profit by a certain date?

The goal shapes the whole plan. A target of 500,000 people trying the product leads to heavy sampling. A target of 100,000 repeat buyers puts the weight on taste, availability and price, because people only buy again if the product is good and easy to find.

The structure

  • Who to target
    • Segment size and growth
    • Competitors in the segment
    • Unmet needs
  • What to offer (the 4Ps)
    • Product
    • Price
    • Place (channels)
    • Promotion (message and brand)
  • How to roll it out
    • Capabilities: production, distribution, cash
    • Pilot, then scale
  • Does it pay?
    • Expected sales
    • Costs and break-even
    • Cannibalisation of existing products

A worked example: a high-protein snack bar

A snack maker wants 100,000 repeat buyers of a new protein bar in year one. All numbers are illustrative.

Step 1: target

Gym-goers and active commuters who already buy protein snacks but complain about taste. That choice drives the rest: flavour testing, gym and station-shop channels, and a price close to the leading brands.

Step 2: work back through the funnel

A pilot in one region shows that 25% of people who try the bar buy it again. To reach 100,000 repeat buyers, the brand needs 100,000 ÷ 25% = 400,000 trial buyers. Now check whether retailers, production and the marketing budget can reach that many people.

Step 3: check it pays

  • Contribution to the maker is $0.60 a bar, after the retailer's margin and production cost.
  • Launch costs (listing fees, sampling, advertising) are $1.2M.
  • Trial buyers buy 2 bars. Repeat buyers buy another 20 during the year.

Bars sold: 400,000 × 2 = 800,000 trial bars, plus 100,000 × 20 = 2,000,000 repeat bars, a total of 2.8M. Contribution: 2.8M × $0.60 = $1.68M, which covers the $1.2M launch cost with $480,000 to spare. About 71% of the bars come from repeat purchases.

Step 4: find the number that matters

At what repeat rate does year one only break even? If the rate is 15%, repeat buyers are 60,000 and buy 1.2M bars. With 800,000 trial bars that is 2.0M bars × $0.60 = $1.2M, exactly the launch cost. So the plan works if the repeat rate stays above 15%, and the pilot should be designed to measure it. Agree that threshold before you expand nationally.

What a strong answer sounds like

"I'd target gym-goers first, because they already buy protein bars and the need is clear. The launch only pays if people come back, so I'd judge it on repeat rate: above 15% we cover the $1.2M launch cost in year one. I'd pilot in one region, measure trial and repeat, and scale only if we clear that bar."

A weak answer jumps to "a big social media campaign and influencers" before saying who the bar is for or how the client will know whether the launch worked.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing price and promotion before the customer. Pick the segment first; the 4Ps follow.
  • Counting trial as success. Repeat purchase is what builds a product. Define the funnel: aware, trial, repeat, retained.
  • Ignoring cannibalisation. Sales taken from the client's own products are not new money.
  • No pilot. Test in one region or channel, with success thresholds agreed in advance.
  • Forgetting capabilities. Can the client make, ship and fund the volume the plan assumes?

Practise it

1. Should a supermarket launch a premium own-label range?

Show the answer
  • Customer demand: shoppers already buying premium brands; whether they trust our brand at that level
  • Economics: margin against branded products; volume needed to cover development
  • Suppliers: who can make it at the right quality; how the big brands react
  • Cannibalisation: sales taken from our standard own-label; net margin gained

Start with margin against branded products, since premium own-label usually earns more per item. The trap is ignoring how big brands might respond, for example by cutting their promotions with us.

2. Should a business school launch a fully online MBA?

Show the answer
  • Demand: students who cannot study on campus; the price they would pay
  • Competition: other online MBAs and their prices; our brand against theirs
  • Economics: development and teaching cost; students needed to break even
  • Cannibalisation and brand: students switching from the campus programme; perceived quality

Start with cannibalisation of the campus MBA, which is usually the school's flagship. The trap is assuming all online students are new.

3. A launch needs 50,000 repeat customers. A pilot shows 20% of people who try it come back. How many trial customers are needed?

Show the answer

50,000 ÷ 20% = 250,000 trial customers. If the repeat rate could be raised to 25% through a better product or price, only 200,000 would be needed, which is often cheaper than buying 50,000 extra trials with advertising.

Where to practise next

Read what to ask first in a product launch case, then try a full case: SnackCo protein bar, or Velisse Skin, where a new refill pouch may eat into bottle sales.
